page_hint: Ch 10, section '8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case', paragraph 2
quoted_clause: they verify the DP gradient-sync (if fine-tuning) stays under ~20% [ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] of step time
observed: The chapter's own ring model makes this check unsatisfiable for the mini-case's 400B model. The check is stated as a routine verification step without noting that the configuration it describes cannot meet it, so a reader either performs an impossible check or silently ignores the chapter's own arithmetic.
evidence: Recomputation with the chapter's formulas: 400e9 params x 4 B = 1,600 GB of FP32 gradients. Ring per-rank send = 2(N-1)/N x 1,600 GB ~ 3,200 GB for large N. At the H100 NVLink directional peak of 450 GB/s: 3,200/450 = 7.1 s per step. At 25 GB/s: 3,200/25 = 128 s per step. A 20% budget therefore requires a step time of >= 35.6 s (NVLink) or >= 640 s (25 GB/s). The mini-case's own TPOT figures (80 ms -> 38 ms) imply a step time on the order of tens of milliseconds.
root_cause: The mini-case reuses the Ch 10 DP heuristic (a ~20% budget) without re-deriving it at the mini-case's model scale, where the gradient object is 5.7x larger than the canonical 70B.
correction: Either state that the fine-tuning path uses sharded DP (FSDP/ZeRO) so the synchronized object is a per-shard gradient rather than a full-replica gradient, or replace the check with the sharded-DP accounting and its own numbers. If the check is retained as-is, add the sentence that it is unsatisfiable at 400B without sharding.
acceptance_test: A reader can compute the gradient-sync time for the mini-case's model from the chapter's own formulas and can state what configuration would bring it under 20% of step time.

page_hint: Ch 10, section '8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case', final sentence
quoted_clause: Moving the cross-node decomposition from TP to PP cuts TPOT from 80 ms to 38 ms [ILLUSTRATIVE], with ~3 ms of the residual being PP stage-boundary and bubble cost under the chosen $P$ and $m$, and the team's "parallelism is slow" becomes a precise, diagnosed, and fixed split.

The phrase 'fixed split' refers to the decomposition, but the sentence's subject ('the team's parallelism is slow') is the latency, which is not fixed.

correction: Either close the gap with a named, mechanism-level step and its own arithmetic (larger m to shrink the bubble; EP to cut the per-layer exchange; speculative decoding to cut steps per token), or state explicitly that the diagnosis is complete and that the residual 13 ms is a separate, named optimization target with an owner and a next measurement.

page_hint: Ch 11, section '3. Worked Example', subsection 'Discrete Batching Wastes the GPU', bullet 2
quoted_clause: The batch is locked until its *slowest* member finishes (the batch runs to completion), so a short 100-token output tails behind the longest while the GPU finishes the whole batch - idle bubbles at the end of every batch.
observed: The bullet names two effects - head-of-line blocking on response delivery, and the drain bubble between batches - but omits the primary GPU-efficiency loss in discrete batching: sequences that finish early keep consuming compute slots (padding to the batch's longest member) until the batch completes. That is the effect continuous batching removes, and it is the one the subsection's own title ('Wastes the GPU') points at.
evidence: The canonical output is ~300 tokens and the bullet's example is a 100-token output - a 3x spread within one batch, which is exactly the regime where padding waste dominates. The bullet's 'idle bubbles at the end of every batch' describes the inter-batch drain, not the intra-batch waste.
root_cause: The bullet conflates 'the GPU is idle' with 'the GPU is doing useless work'; only the former is described.
correction: Add the padding-waste effect explicitly and distinguish it from the drain bubble: finished sequences occupy slots and consume compute until the batch's longest member completes, and separately the GPU drains between batches.
acceptance_test: The discrete-batching subsection names at least three distinct costs and identifies which one continuous batching removes and which it does not.

page_hint: Ch 12, §1 'Concept', para. 4 (page not determinable from chunk)
quoted_clause: as a single host falls against the canonical ~92K input tokens/s
observed: The figure is used as a canonical threshold, but the chunk never states whether it is a per-host capacity or a fleet-level demand, nor the model, precision, host count, or MFU behind it. Under the capacity reading it is arithmetically impossible on the substrate this same chunk fixes; under the demand reading it contradicts the canonical workload's peak input-token rate established in Ch 11's mini-case.
evidence: Canonical model is pinned by this chunk: 70B full-MHA FP16 (KV 2.62 MB/token; 9.2K tokens -> 24.1 GB, 9.5K -> 24.9 GB). Canonical host is pinned by this chunk: 8xH100. Prefill FLOPs/token for a 70B model at 9.2K context ~ 2x70e9 + attention (~4x80x8192x9200 = 2.4e10) ~ 1.64e11. 8xH100 FP16 dense = 8 x 989 TFLOPS = 7.91e15 FLOP/s => <=48.2K tok/s at 100% MFU, and 19-24K tok/s at a realistic 40-50% MFU. FP8 dense (1,979 TFLOPS/H100) => 96.5K tok/s at 100% MFU, so 92K would require ~95% MFU. Demand reading: Ch 11 mini-case fixes the canonical service peak at 40 rps and the canonical request at 9.2K input tokens => 40 x 9,200 = 368K input tokens/s at peak, 4x the 92K figure.
root_cause: A canonical throughput value was carried across chapters without a stated scope (capacity vs. demand), model, precision, or MFU, and without reconciliation against the canonical workload's own token-rate arithmetic.
correction: State explicitly what 92K is. If it is a per-host prefill capacity, re-derive it from the canonical model, precision, host count, and an explicit MFU and correct the number (for 70B on 8xH100 FP16 the ceiling is ~48K tok/s at 100% MFU). If it is a demand, state the request rate and input length that produce it and reconcile it with 40 rps x 9.2K = 368K input tokens/s from Ch 11's mini-case. Add the derivation, or a cross-reference to the chapter that holds it, at first use.
acceptance_test: From the text alone a reader can state (a) whether 92K input tokens/s is a per-host capacity or a fleet demand, (b) the model, precision, host count, and MFU that produce it, and (c) the arithmetic reconciling it with 40 rps x 9.2K input tokens/s. If any of the three is unavailable, the figure is not publication-ready.
